lesson.title: A Nation at War With Its Own Citizens' Rights
lesson.summary: Fear and racism following Pearl Harbor led the U.S. government to forcibly remove and incarcerate roughly 120,000 people of Japanese descent, most of them American citizens, in one of the most serious violations of civil liberties in U.S. history.
lesson.body:
The shock and fear that followed the attack on Pearl Harbor did not stay confined to the battlefield. On the West Coast, longstanding anti-Asian prejudice combined with wartime panic to produce demands that people of Japanese ancestry be treated as security threats, even though no evidence of espionage or sabotage by Japanese Americans was ever found. Military and political leaders, under pressure from West Coast politicians and the public, pushed for drastic action against a population that had committed no crime.

On February 19, 1942, President Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, authorizing the military to designate areas from which any persons could be excluded. The order did not name Japanese Americans specifically, but it was applied almost entirely to them. Over the following months, the government forcibly removed roughly 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry from their homes along the West Coast, giving many families only days to sell or abandon homes, farms, and businesses built over decades. About two-thirds of those removed were Nisei, American-born citizens with full constitutional rights, and many others were Issei immigrants who had lived in the United States for years but had been barred by earlier law from becoming naturalized citizens.

Those removed were sent first to hastily built temporary assembly centers, often at fairgrounds or racetracks, and then to more permanent camps run by the War Relocation Authority in remote, harsh locations such as Manzanar and Tule Lake in California, Heart Mountain in Wyoming, and Topaz in Utah. Families lived in barracks behind barbed wire, guarded by armed soldiers, for up to three years, with no charges filed and no trials held. It was, in plain terms, imprisonment based on ancestry rather than any individual wrongdoing.

Even amid this injustice, thousands of young Japanese American men volunteered or were drafted for military service, some directly out of the camps. The 442nd Regimental Combat Team, made up almost entirely of Japanese American soldiers, fought with extraordinary distinction in Europe and became one of the most highly decorated units in U.S. Army history relative to its size. It was not until decades later, with the Civil Liberties Act of 1988, that the federal government formally apologized for internment and provided reparations payments to surviving victims, officially acknowledging what historians and the government's own later review had already concluded: that the policy had been driven by 'race prejudice, war hysteria, and a failure of political leadership,' not military necessity.
